title: Vayetze: leaving town (Genesis 28:10)
hook: Rashi: when a good person leaves a town, its beauty leaves with them

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esau's bitter cry, bless me, even me also. Your line was the loser's tears count. Today, a new portion, and Jacob on the run.

A coworker retires on a Friday. The one who remembered birthdays, who made the bad coffee a little better, who laughed at everything. On Monday it's the same building, the same desks. But something has gone out of the place, and it stays gone for weeks. This week's portion is called Vayetze, and he went out. Esau is furious and wants his brother dead, so Rebekah and Isaac send Jacob away, to her family in Haran. He leaves home with nothing but a staff.
screen: `THE OFFICE AFTER SHE RETIRED.` → `VAYETZE: AND HE WENT OUT.` → `JACOB LEAVES WITH A STAFF.`

segments.voice: The portion opens with a short verse: Jacob went out from Beer-sheba, and went toward Haran. Rashi, the medieval teacher from France, read it slowly and asked a simple question. The verse could have said only that Jacob went toward Haran. Why mention that he left Beer-sheba at all? The words should earn their place. Rashi's answer, drawn from an old midrash, is lovely. When a good person leaves a place, it makes an impression. While they live in a town, they are its glory, its brightness, its beauty. When they go, the glory, the brightness and the beauty go with them. Now notice who it's about. Jacob, right now, isn't a hero. He's just deceived his father and fled his brother. And still, the rabbis say, Beer-sheba was a little dimmer the morning he left. Rashi even asks: but Isaac was still there, wasn't he? And he answers, more or less: one good person is not the same as two. Every good person counts, and one leaving still leaves a gap. It turns a familiar idea around, that places make people: a good neighborhood, a good school. Rashi is saying the opposite is at least as true. People make places. The quiet ones, too, who hold the door and know everyone's kids' names. You often don't know what they were until the morning after they've gone.
screen: `JACOB WENT OUT FROM BEER-SHEBA.` · `WHY SAY HE LEFT?` · `THE GLORY, BRIGHTNESS AND BEAUTY GO.` · `EVERY GOOD PERSON COUNTS.` · then, large: `PEOPLE MAKE PLACES.`

segments.voice: Picture a place you're in every week: your street, your work, your building, your prayer community, your gym. Now picture it without the one person who makes it a little warmer, and feel what would go out of the room. Hold their face in mind for a moment, with gratitude.
Vayetze. And he went out: the portion that opens with Jacob leaving home, and a town a little dimmer without him.
Your line: people make places. Beer-sheba felt it the very morning Jacob left. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vayetze is read in synagogues each late autumn, and Rashi's commentary is commonly printed beside the Torah text for study.
